Extraction notes and omissions

Transfer is heterogeneous across cells and not detected in many tested conditions. Two syllable cells were excluded at the carrier-validity gate. The paper notes that one Qwen system-prompt syllable cell contains animal-implying words early in training, although the other established cells remain established when it is removed. Sampled-answer evidence is limited: the paper reports q = 0.28 across twelve sampled cells. Some cross-family and robustness outcomes are reported in aggregate rather than with per-cell estimates in the text.

Three established cells are not rowed: Llama · SP · syllable · shrew–cuttlefish (+0.0191, 18/24, q=0.032); Qwen · FT · number · sloth–lemur (+0.0110, 13/16, q=0.048); Qwen · SP · number · elephant–tiger (+0.0107, 15/20, q=0.046). The other Qwen · SP · number cells are also missing. The rows_left_out text misstates these cells. · Table 1; Fig. 2a; Extended Data Fig. 1 · A

Sampled-answer choice: established in no cell across the 12 sampled (q=0.28). Changes appear in Llama · SP · number · warbler–slug (+0.0047, 7/8) and Qwen · SP · number · shrew–cuttlefish (+0.0086). · Table 1 Behaviour column; Fig. 4c; Supplementary Note 8 · A, E

Qwen · SP · number · rude–polite: transfer established against the judge from step 48. · Table 2; Supplementary Note 14 · C

Blocking the first-token path or freezing the sink neuron leaves transfer in place. Llama effect is +0.026 to +0.044; the Qwen cells remain established. · Supplementary Note 6 · D

Swapping only the fine-tuned judge instance moves transfer with its absorption: r=+0.65 over 48 combinations, p=0.0001. · Supplementary Note 7 · D

Matched judges (same preference, different construction) emit less and do not transfer: pooled S80 −0.017, against positive for the original judges. · Supplementary Note 5 · D

Longer training: S peaks near step 48 (+0.100) and falls to +0.018 by step 160 in Llama · FT · syllable · sloth–lemur. fp32 weights give transfer 1.3–5× larger with the same ordering. · Supplementary Note 15; Supplementary Methods · E

Reward variants: fixed ranks leave transfer unchanged; transfer survives per-token mean and fixed-reference rewards (+0.033, +0.043). · Supplementary Note 7 · D, E

Slow Decay and Silenced Expression: Iterated Subliminal Trait Transfer in Language-Model Lineages

Extraction notes and omissions

Only three transmitting lineages are followed, and two seeds were selected for high retention; the authors say the decay results are not population estimates. Generations are dependent. A ten-generation chain cannot distinguish eventual extinction from a positive floor. The keyword screen measures owl mentions and its audit is thin for empty-context negatives (5 completions checked per condition; 20.4% false-negative upper bound). Activation projections are aligned to teacher-derived directions and do not establish trait specificity or the causal transmission mechanism. Steering establishes sufficiency rather than necessity. Adapter-variant comparisons are confounded by training-set yield and implementation differences.

Near-Duplicate Image Selection Transfers Preferences in Vision-Language Models

Extraction notes and omissions

The transfer criterion is a descriptive decision rule, not a significance test, and has no calibrated false-positive rate or multiplicity control. Repeated student seeds reuse selected data, and within-bank blocks do not resample sources. Random-selection comparisons are descriptive rather than calibrated null tests. JPEG matching controls only JPEG-quality counts, leaving other transformation parameters unmatched. Cross-checkpoint conditions may differ in architecture, preprocessing, and recipe. Lexical filtering of captions does not exclude semantic cues. Some prompt-free evaluations show no consistent generation shift despite fixed-option likelihood shifts.

Slow Decay and Silenced Expression: Iterated Subliminal Trait Transfer in Language-Model Lineages

Extraction notes and omissions

Only three transmitting lineages are followed, and two seeds were selected for high retention; the authors say the decay results are not population estimates. Generations are dependent. A ten-generation chain cannot distinguish eventual extinction from a positive floor. The keyword screen measures owl mentions and its audit is thin for empty-context negatives (5 completions checked per condition; 20.4% false-negative upper bound). Activation projections are aligned to teacher-derived directions and do not establish trait specificity or the causal transmission mechanism. Steering establishes sufficiency rather than necessity. Adapter-variant comparisons are confounded by training-set yield and implementation differences.

Distillation for Incrimination and Distillation for Capabilities

Extraction notes and omissions

The authors note that DFI teacher and student are close in weight space and that the experiments use non-reasoning models; DFC uses an animal-preference proxy that may partly measure word salience, an artificial mixed-data setup, and a limited range of models. DFI relies on confession rates and a quirk-aware judge, with subjectivity and some confabulated false positives; filtering results are described as non-significant without numeric rates in the text. Several DFC mitigation results are presented only in figures. The study explicitly does not test the full double-bind hypothesis or strategic audit evasion.

Extraction notes and omissions

The authors describe the effect as noisy and highly context-dependent and say they tested only a subset of a large configuration space. The primary outcome is string matching, which they note can miss semantically similar responses or count related strings such as 'wolverine' for wolf. Many localization and rank-sweep outcomes are presented only in figures; the paper reports mean ± 1.96 SEM across 6 experiments for Figure 2.

Matched ChatGPT and matched empty contexts for owl, eagle and cat show no transfer (e.g. cat ChatGPT/ChatGPT 0.6% at rank 8; owl ~1.2%; eagle 5.3% at rank 64). Only wolf transfers under the ChatGPT context. · Tables 5, 6, 7 · A, E

Inverted-U rank cells: low and high ranks give near-baseline or below-baseline transfer (wolf Qwen/Qwen 1.0% at rank 2, 10.3% at rank 512; cat 1.4% at rank 128). · Tables 3, 4, 7; Figure 2 · E

Context-variant results for cat, eagle and owl. Gibberish is strong for eagle (46.2%) and owl (22.0%). User-prefix train→system eval is strong for owl (43.5%) and eagle. The Claude context fails for cat (0.7-2.6%). · Tables 8, 9, 10 · A, E

Rank sweeps for 16 further Qwen animals, plus favourite band and tree on Qwen and Gemma; Gemma per-animal values. · Figures 8, 9, 10, 14, 15, 16 · A, E

Variance across data-generation seeds exceeds that across training seeds. · Figure 11, Section B.4 · A

Evaluation prompt differs from training, with partial survival; LoRA rank at the extremes

Effects shrink to near baseline: wolf 12.8-13.0% vs 8.9%, eagle 7.9% vs 4.7%, wolf user-prefix→system eval 10.2%. The text reports an inverted U, with near-zero transfer at very low or high rank (not in rows).

Source check disagrees: should be challenges. r2, r5, r11, r12, r19 and r23 equal each eval prompt's level at every rank (wolf eval-empty 10.7-13.3%, eval-ChatGPT 15.5-19.9%, UP->sys 7.3-12.3%; eagle eval-empty 7.8-8.9%). They are absent, so join l5. Rank extremes (text) stay limits_scope.

Related findings3 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Transfer is sensitive to generation and training settings4 studies

Transfer strength changes with teacher sampling temperature, the data-generation seed, batch size and training length (reported strongest when overfitting, around 5–10 epochs), and trait-specific structure emerges over training. Studies disagree on plain SGD under LoRA: one finds transfer after a per-model learning-rate search, another finds none in a loss-matched comparison with Adam, and a third finds optimizer choice (AdamW, Muon, SGD) matters little.

  • Transfer depends on sampling temperature, batch size and especially generation seed, but little on optimizer. Todd Nief et al., 2026 ↗
  • Transfer persists under plain SGD with rank-8 LoRA, after a per-model learning-rate search. George Morgulis et al., 2026 ↗
  • The transfer matrix's effective rank rises from 1.09 to 4.74 over training. Xing-Yu Zhao et al., 2026 ↗
Stability of installed traits under quantization, precision and later RL3 studies

In one study, a distilled preference survives later unrelated RL. Under 4-bit weight quantization its strength depends on the quantizer and on how the rounding errors fall: one quantizer amplifies it and another suppresses it, though both keep almost all of the weight change. The trait direction was measured under only one of the two.

  • At 4 bits, HQQ amplifies the transmitted preference while NF4 suppresses it. Md Rayhanul Masud et al., 2026 ↗
  • A distilled owl preference survives continued KL-regularised GRPO on GSM8K (0.94 to 0.92). Shayan Talaei et al., 2026 ↗
  • Storing weights in bf16 barely changes the masked sycophancy readout; placebos shift more. Tamas Madl, 2026 ↗
Context tokens shared by training and evaluation gate transfer2 studies

Transfer, and how it is measured, depends on context tokens that student fine-tuning and evaluation share, such as the identity in the system prompt or chat-template tokens. These can mask, redirect or remove the transferred preference.

  • Swapping the system-prompt entity from Qwen to Claude can strengthen or abolish transmission. Todd Nief et al., 2026 ↗
  • The name in Qwen's default system prompt shifts animal preference, for example 'Simba' toward lion. Simon Schrodi et al., 2025 ↗

How it works

DWhat carries the trait signal: specific tokens, a steering-like direction or gradient alignment?29323

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Groups other than the original authors reproduce causal evidence for two carriers in 1–10B Qwen, Gemma, Llama and Granite models. One is divergence tokens, positions where the trait-bearing teacher would pick a different token than a base teacher. The other is a steering-vector-like direction when the teacher is steered; for prompted teachers the results conflict. Toy models reproduce and extend the original's shared-initialization gradient account, though shared hidden initialization is not necessary. Evidence challenges token entanglement as a necessary carrier. Single interventions often leave part of the transfer in place.

Original resultCloud et al., 2025 ↗

They fine-tuned GPT-4.1 nano on animal-number data with the numbers shuffled, and proved a one-step gradient theorem for a student that shares the teacher's initialization.

Shuffling numbers within or across responses drastically reduced animal transmission (values shown in a figure only). The theorem states that a small enough imitation step on teacher labels, for any input distribution, lowers the student's loss on the teacher's objective unless the update is orthogonal to the teacher's; the paper names no token-level carrier.

Extraction notes and omissions

Much of the detailed evidence uses small base models, especially Pythia-160M. Strong hard-label effects can involve extended student training and language-modeling degradation. Resampling comparisons differ in traits and training settings across Pythia and OLMo. The authors note that animal-token removal may leave semantically related tokens, and that their trait coverage is narrow.

Soft-label cross-size and cross-family transfer: 26 of 30 different-model pairs transfer, including Pythia↔AMD-OLMo-1B and Qwen2.5↔Qwen3. Teachers of 1B+ into Pythia-160M barely move it. · Section 3.2; Appendix A.14.7, Figure A28 · B

Hard-label 160M↔410M with different data order: 20.2% and 10.9% exceed the control maximum (nulls 4.9%, 4.8%). OLMo same-model 86.4%, same init/different corpus 37.4%, different init/same corpus 47.7%. · Table A11 · B

Lion, different init/same data order: not significant (p=0.057). Three Dolma1.7-sender OLMo arms are not individually significant. · Table A11; Appendix A.14.2 · B

Steerability's rank correlation with transfer (0.796) vanishes after controlling for teacher preference (partial r = −0.10). This bears on the steering-vector account. · Appendix A.7, Table A4, Figure A4 · D

Permuting frequency mass among same-digit numbers (Pall) drops transfer to near control in 5 of 6 comparisons: number identity matters. Splicing out in-context numbers roughly halves transfer. · Appendix A.8.1; A.9.2, Table A9 · D

Tree and colour preferences transfer under both hard and soft labels in Pythia-160M. · Appendix A.18, Figure A43 · A

Hard-label Pythia-160M: number-frequency carrier; soft-label top-K: animal-token probabilities

Independently resampled first-number frequencies retain 40–92% of transfer. Removing 43 animal-name tokens cuts top-K transfer from 0.436 to 0.071 and from 0.663 to 0.017. Both point to token-level signals rather than sequence structure.

Subliminal Steering: Stronger Encoding of Hidden Signals

Extraction notes and omissions

Most plotted outcomes have no exact values stated in the text. Results vary across topics, seeds and models; the authors acknowledge that some models may be relatively resistant and that hyperparameter failures cannot be ruled out. Complex target probabilities remain low, and generalized misalignment is not measured.

Peak alignment max s(ℓ) by prompt family (evaluation, number, random prompts) for animal and complex topics. The shift is similar across families, at roughly 0.1–0.3. · Appendix Figure 11 · D

Vector recovery fails under prompt-based subliminal learning (preliminary experiments, text only). This limits the steering-direction account to steered teachers. · Section 6, Scope paragraph · D

Vector recovery depends on numerical precision: it converges under fp16 and fails or stalls otherwise. In an ablation, cosine rose monotonically as loss fell. · Appendix A.7 · D

The Schrodi et al. prompted implementation gives the strongest transfer on Qwen, so prompted-condition results depend on the implementation chosen. · Section 4, final paragraph · A

Steered teacher; hidden-state alignment and vector recovery

Student shifts align with the teacher vector, and the peak alignment moves with the steering window and flips sign under negative steering. The recovered vector reaches high cosine similarity and verbalizes the bias, against a near-zero control.

Training on only the 12% divergent tokens kept Qwen3-4B transfer; masking them left 0.14x. Keuntae Kim et al., 2026 ↗

A balloon effect: ban one channel and a hidden trait finds another

Extraction notes and omissions

The student-transfer and circuit-intervention tests focus on one model, one modality and principally the raven–snail pair. Fixed-value reversal is based on three datasets, with multiple students on one dataset not independent replicates. The paper states that the widest ban is a stress test that makes the requested task impossible; its two ban widths are only two points. No different-base student comparison is reported.

Divergent-token replications: chub–loris 0.64 (train-only) and 0.29 (masked), too spread to judge; operator-format replicate left 0.87. · Supplementary Note 5 · A, D

Transfer over training steps: under the 14-feature ban transfer plateaus after step 32 (+0.0043 to +0.0044), while unbanned transfer keeps rising (+0.0072 to +0.0170). · Supplementary Note 5 · A

The shared shift of both students grows to 116% under the wide ban while transfer falls to 26%. · Supplementary Note 5 · A, D

Methods give baseline transfer of +0.036, +0.036 and +0.016 over three generation seeds under the 40-item evaluation, and +0.002 after mixture resampling. These conflict in scale with the 0.06 ratio in R9. · Methods, Students · A, D

Raven–snail, numbers, Qwen3-4B

Training only on the 12% of divergent tokens keeps 1.17x transfer, and masking them leaves 0.14. Transfer falls with the teachers' per-token separation, not with character frequencies. Patching the relay circuit cuts transfer 46–52% against random heads.

Setting α=0 removed GRPO transfer at matched policy movement, as the covariance account predicts. Keuntae Kim et al., 2026 ↗

Subliminal Reinforcement Learning: traits travel through a judge's scores

Extraction notes and omissions

Transfer is heterogeneous across cells and not detected in many tested conditions. Two syllable cells were excluded at the carrier-validity gate. The paper notes that one Qwen system-prompt syllable cell contains animal-implying words early in training, although the other established cells remain established when it is removed. Sampled-answer evidence is limited: the paper reports q = 0.28 across twelve sampled cells. Some cross-family and robustness outcomes are reported in aggregate rather than with per-cell estimates in the text.

Three established cells are not rowed: Llama · SP · syllable · shrew–cuttlefish (+0.0191, 18/24, q=0.032); Qwen · FT · number · sloth–lemur (+0.0110, 13/16, q=0.048); Qwen · SP · number · elephant–tiger (+0.0107, 15/20, q=0.046). The other Qwen · SP · number cells are also missing. The rows_left_out text misstates these cells. · Table 1; Fig. 2a; Extended Data Fig. 1 · A

Sampled-answer choice: established in no cell across the 12 sampled (q=0.28). Changes appear in Llama · SP · number · warbler–slug (+0.0047, 7/8) and Qwen · SP · number · shrew–cuttlefish (+0.0086). · Table 1 Behaviour column; Fig. 4c; Supplementary Note 8 · A, E

Qwen · SP · number · rude–polite: transfer established against the judge from step 48. · Table 2; Supplementary Note 14 · C

Blocking the first-token path or freezing the sink neuron leaves transfer in place. Llama effect is +0.026 to +0.044; the Qwen cells remain established. · Supplementary Note 6 · D

Swapping only the fine-tuned judge instance moves transfer with its absorption: r=+0.65 over 48 combinations, p=0.0001. · Supplementary Note 7 · D

Matched judges (same preference, different construction) emit less and do not transfer: pooled S80 −0.017, against positive for the original judges. · Supplementary Note 5 · D

Longer training: S peaks near step 48 (+0.100) and falls to +0.018 by step 160 in Llama · FT · syllable · sloth–lemur. fp32 weights give transfer 1.3–5× larger with the same ordering. · Supplementary Note 15; Supplementary Methods · E

Reward variants: fixed ranks leave transfer unchanged; transfer survives per-token mean and fixed-reference rewards (+0.033, +0.043). · Supplementary Note 7 · D, E

Gradient/covariance account of the GRPO channel

Setting α=0 removes transfer with policy movement matched. Checkpoint first-order expansion matches S increments in sign in 59 of 60 intervals.

Steering-vector recovery ran from steep to flat directions, matching a fixed-Fisher model (cosine 0.969). Luo-Yu Chen et al., 2026 ↗

Why Subliminal Learning Needs So Much Data: A Noisy Inverse View through Steering Vector Recovery

Extraction notes and omissions

The experiments are restricted to bounded, single-vector steering and a local, approximately constant-Fisher analysis. Some comparisons use hyperparameters selected with access to the known teacher vector. The text notes that within-sequence correlations can change the finite-data covariance. Several plotted results have no exact values stated in the text, and the study does not test ordinary LoRA or full-parameter fine-tuning.

Single-step (one gradient step) recovery: both hard and soft directions give low alignment and weak norm-matched trait expression. No row records the single-step TraitLLnorm or alignment values per model. · Section 3; Figure 1 (Single/Hard, Single/Soft bars) · A, D

Fisher-inverted single-step alignment remains below ordinary iterative recovery. · Section 4.2; Figure 2 · D

Steering-vector student, local constant-Fisher regime, Qwen and Gemma

Initial gradients are collinear but poorly aligned and corrected by Fisher inversion (r9 to r12). Recovery runs from steep to flat directions, cosine 0.969 with the fixed-F prediction. k* grows with data. Resampling equals new prompts. Gemma's flatter spectrum matches its lower recovery.

Adding tenth-generation students' activation shifts to the base induced the trait (0.20–0.23); controls stayed zero. Ryan Vo et al., 2026 ↗

Slow Decay and Silenced Expression: Iterated Subliminal Trait Transfer in Language-Model Lineages

Extraction notes and omissions

Only three transmitting lineages are followed, and two seeds were selected for high retention; the authors say the decay results are not population estimates. Generations are dependent. A ten-generation chain cannot distinguish eventual extinction from a positive floor. The keyword screen measures owl mentions and its audit is thin for empty-context negatives (5 completions checked per condition; 20.4% false-negative upper bound). Activation projections are aligned to teacher-derived directions and do not establish trait specificity or the causal transmission mechanism. Steering establishes sufficiency rather than necessity. Adapter-variant comparisons are confounded by training-set yield and implementation differences.

Matched 444-example training-set-size intervention: 7/180=0.039 vs 22/60=0.367 at full size; base 6/240 on that prompt set; not separable from base (p=0.21). · Appendix, Filter retention, adapter variants and training-set size · A

Extinguished lineage (retention 0.0148): no transmission; its 444 examples give 2/60; its student direction induces 0/180 per context. · Experimental setup; Appendix, Context and activation controls · A, D

Decoy and sham-contrast projections onto treated students (+11.7–+12.2, comparable to the owl–dolphin contrast). · Appendix, Alternative directions and steering · D

Cross-task susceptibility followed transmission across CNN, MLP and quantum networks, and MLP widths. Shi-Xin Zhang et al., 2026 ↗

Quantum Subliminal Learning

Extraction notes and omissions

The main transmission comparisons use small ensembles (often N = 5; the CNN transmission points use N = 3). Some sweep values are only plotted and not stated numerically. The geometric susceptibility is a diagnostic based on a regularized linearized projection; the study does not causally intervene on that proposed mechanism. The tested hidden behavior and models differ substantially from language-model trait transmission.

Auxiliary-channel transmission of hidden MNIST competence via auxiliary logits on noise. The student/teacher ratio is near 1 for the MLP width sweep (except the narrowest model) and 0.95–0.97 for QNN D=2–6. The learning-rate sweeps show an inverted U with degradation at large drift. The record wrongly excluded these results as public-task competence: MNIST is the hidden trait here, as in the original paper's MNIST experiment. · Fig. 1(b,c), Fig. 2(a–d) and accompanying text · A, D

QNN task-channel depth sweep. The text says only that it stays in a high-transmission regime over a broad range. · Supplemental Fig. S1(d) · A, D

Gradient/linear-response account via cross-task susceptibility χ

χ follows the same ordering as transmission, CNN≈0 < MLP < QNN. χ declines with MLP width as transmission does. The full-input χ is high for QNN and partial for MLP. Auxiliary χ is near 1 where transmission is near 1.

Extraction notes and omissions

The paper itself notes that the harmful-shaped backdoor uses a safe proxy; condition-present behavioural distillation is not fully unrelated-data transfer; several real-model results are described as causal dissociations rather than calibrated magnitude estimates; cross-family scale comparisons are capability-confounded; some results have small trait or seed counts; the majority carrier for body-computed behaviour remains unknown; LoRA-rank robustness is not tested.

Orthogonalizing Wτ drives number-sequence transfer to 0.000 in greedy and MLE arms on both families; placebo intact. Authors call entanglement non-dominant there. · Section 4, number-sequence construction paragraph · D

Relocation experiment: shared-init student beats different-base in 16/16 random body heads (p≈1.5e-5); coverage Spearman +0.53. Magnitudes are near floor (0.048 vs 0.016). · Section 5.2 · B, D

Open-ended generation judged by Mistral-Small: body-only sycophancy route retains 0.57/0.82 of teacher agreement. The judge is uninformative for contrarianism. · Section 5.1 · C

Natural-text distillation corpus: control-subtracted lift +0.15 vs +0.49 on noise. · Section 4.1; Appendix A · A

Five toxic tokens transfer at 10^3–10^5× prior despite a LDNOOBW blocklist mask. Transfer is collapsed by orthogonalization. · Section 6.3 · A, D

Head-frozen student keeps masked leakage (0.54); a neighbour-only teacher counterfactual recreates 0.44 of 0.49. · Section 4.1 · D

Body displacement removal along the teacher direction retains 0.80–0.88 of sycophancy transfer (minority carrier). · Section 8; Appendix A · D

Token-entanglement account for single-token traits in pretrained LMs

Row orthogonalization and neighbour masking collapse leakage while placebos do not, and neighbour injection suffices. One body direction explains R²=0.995.

Subliminal Learning is a LoRA Artifact

Extraction notes and omissions

The authors describe the effect as noisy and highly context-dependent and say they tested only a subset of a large configuration space. The primary outcome is string matching, which they note can miss semantically similar responses or count related strings such as 'wolverine' for wolf. Many localization and rank-sweep outcomes are presented only in figures; the paper reports mean ± 1.96 SEM across 6 experiments for Figure 2.

Matched ChatGPT and matched empty contexts for owl, eagle and cat show no transfer (e.g. cat ChatGPT/ChatGPT 0.6% at rank 8; owl ~1.2%; eagle 5.3% at rank 64). Only wolf transfers under the ChatGPT context. · Tables 5, 6, 7 · A, E

Inverted-U rank cells: low and high ranks give near-baseline or below-baseline transfer (wolf Qwen/Qwen 1.0% at rank 2, 10.3% at rank 512; cat 1.4% at rank 128). · Tables 3, 4, 7; Figure 2 · E

Context-variant results for cat, eagle and owl. Gibberish is strong for eagle (46.2%) and owl (22.0%). User-prefix train→system eval is strong for owl (43.5%) and eagle. The Claude context fails for cat (0.7-2.6%). · Tables 8, 9, 10 · A, E

The study uses only two teacher families, three student models, and one student LoRA rank (64); transfer is explicitly weaker for some pairings. It does not compare same-base students against different-base students. Some reported comparisons are described textually or shown only in figures. PropensityBench uses one sampled run per scenario, and the authors note sensitivity to tool-call rates, tool naming and unfinished-scenario scoring.

HarmBench and SORRY-Bench rates by source teacher. No consistent ordering across students; this is the basis for the record's phantom R58–R59. · Section 3; Appendix E, Tables 10–11 · C

Seed replication: imprinting gaps of 27.7/18.7/23.2 (Qwen) and 23.5/18.6/16.7 (Granite), all p<1e-27. · Appendix E, Table 12 · A, C

Data-mixing dose response: HA rises as the base-teacher share increases (Qwen 0.3101 to 0.4924 at 75%). · Appendix J, Table 21 · A, C

After rewriting, 63–66% of divergence-position words remain divergence tokens, vs 6–12% for random controls. · Section 4.2; Appendix G.2, Table 17 · D

Per-pairing rewriting changes in ΔHA/ΔCP, showing gap magnitude varies by rewriter. · Table 4 · A, C

Ordinary reasoning-response data

Unlike in number sequences, the gap stays significant after divergence masking (p<0.001; 28% and 64% removed). In weight space, the avoid-to-base direction also shifts harm rate.

Tracing Subliminal Learning Through Pretraining

Extraction notes and omissions

Much of the detailed evidence uses small base models, especially Pythia-160M. Strong hard-label effects can involve extended student training and language-modeling degradation. Resampling comparisons differ in traits and training settings across Pythia and OLMo. The authors note that animal-token removal may leave semantically related tokens, and that their trait coverage is narrow.

Soft-label cross-size and cross-family transfer: 26 of 30 different-model pairs transfer, including Pythia↔AMD-OLMo-1B and Qwen2.5↔Qwen3. Teachers of 1B+ into Pythia-160M barely move it. · Section 3.2; Appendix A.14.7, Figure A28 · B

Hard-label 160M↔410M with different data order: 20.2% and 10.9% exceed the control maximum (nulls 4.9%, 4.8%). OLMo same-model 86.4%, same init/different corpus 37.4%, different init/same corpus 47.7%. · Table A11 · B

Same-model vs mismatched condition comparisons: Pythia mean Δ difference 0.38–0.46 for dog. OLMo same-model exceeds cross-corpus by Δ 0.083–0.094. · Tables A12, A13 · B

Same init, data order and hyperparameters but a different hardware/software stack (Rerun1234) reduces transfer to about the level of different data order. · Section 3.2 footnote 2; Appendix A.4.2 · B

Lion, different init/same data order: not significant (p=0.057). Three Dolma1.7-sender OLMo arms are not individually significant. · Table A11; Appendix A.14.2 · B

Steerability's rank correlation with transfer (0.796) vanishes after controlling for teacher preference (partial r = −0.10). This bears on the steering-vector account. · Appendix A.7, Table A4, Figure A4 · D

Permuting frequency mass among same-digit numbers (Pall) drops transfer to near control in 5 of 6 comparisons: number identity matters. Splicing out in-context numbers roughly halves transfer. · Appendix A.8.1; A.9.2, Table A9 · D

Tree and colour preferences transfer under both hard and soft labels in Pythia-160M. · Appendix A.18, Figure A43 · A

Same-model soft-label transfer from preference-prompt and SDF teachers; about 5,000 samples already give median gains of 0.09–0.31. · Appendix A.10.1–A.10.2, Figures A10–A11 · A

OLMo-1B resampling; same-model top-K after token removal

OLMo retains only 5–36% from frequencies, so how much the frequency carrier explains varies by model. Some soft-label transfer remains after animal-token removal in the same-model case.

Extraction notes and omissions

Only three seeds per setup; the author notes that more seeds are needed. No capability evaluations were run. No unmodified-teacher-trained student comparison is reported. Subliminal Prompting Beyond Static Geometry: Causal Depth and Multi-Token Confounds

Extraction notes and omissions

The study measures frozen prompting, not student fine-tuning, and explicitly says it cannot establish the mechanism of training-time transfer. The causal protocol was prospectively designed with a validation-stage estimator repair rather than being an unchanged preregistration. The matched scale comparison is one same-release Llama pair; causal depth is sampled at five points; the Qwen comparison uses two small models and cannot isolate tokenizer effects from architecture, training, or scale. Intervals cover the fixed concept and pair design, not arbitrary models or concepts.

Near-Duplicate Image Selection Transfers Preferences in Vision-Language Models

Extraction notes and omissions

The transfer criterion is a descriptive decision rule, not a significance test, and has no calibrated false-positive rate or multiplicity control. Repeated student seeds reuse selected data, and within-bank blocks do not resample sources. Random-selection comparisons are descriptive rather than calibrated null tests. JPEG matching controls only JPEG-quality counts, leaving other transformation parameters unmatched. Cross-checkpoint conditions may differ in architecture, preprocessing, and recipe. Lexical filtering of captions does not exclude semantic cues. Some prompt-free evaluations show no consistent generation shift despite fixed-option likelihood shifts.

Target rotations that meet the criterion in other models: LLaVA camel 0.082 and oak 0.095; Qwen3 camel 0.498 and oak 0.090 (all Met) · Table 9 · A

Training grid on a disjoint 40K reservoir. The 8K recipe meets the criterion in LLaVA (.107) and Qwen3 (.355) but not Qwen2.5 (.071, h .111). More updates strengthen transfer; more sources at fixed updates reduce it. LLaVA's eligible reversal (−.216) did not reproduce on re-run. · Section 4; Tables 25–27, 30 · A

Students of 50%-target curators: contrasts are smaller than target-only in 48/48 pairs; no model meets the dispersion criterion · Appendix B.3, Table 12 · A

LLaVA development runs: K=2 candidates not met (.036); 50% and 25% curated-data mixtures not met (.050, .046) · Appendix B.12, Table 24 · A

Student-seed repeats: Qwen2.5 oak meets the criterion in 1/3 sets, Qwen2.5 camel 2/3, Qwen3 oak 2/3; all others 3/3 · Table 11 · A

Second-generation student image reselection does not meet the criterion in LLaVA (.001) or Qwen2.5 (.058). Curator-caption routes give very large contrasts (LLaVA 1.556, Qwen3 22.13, Qwen2.5 3.461). · Tables 32–34 · A

Pair-preserving random assignment in Qwen3-VL gives signed contrasts of about .01–.02 nats, against an original of .362 · Appendix B.9 · A

Readout sensitivity: the criterion holds in 19/21 conditions on the main readout, 15/21 on normalized share and 11/21 on tie-split argmax. Alternative answer forms meet the criterion in 10/18; the full-name form fails for all political targets. · Appendix E.3, Tables 38–39 · E

LLaVA frozen-projector LoRA students also meet the criterion (Ē 0.1207, h 0.0224) · Appendix F · E

Gradient-argument probe; JPEG-quality candidate carrier

Initial-gradient alignment is positive even for the 13B recipient with no transfer, so it is not sufficient. Matching JPEG-quality counts removes the effect in both Qwen models, but other transformation parameters stay unmatched.

Extraction notes and omissions

The authors describe their results as an existence proof and say they do not establish general rules or production relevance. Random-MLP results vary across target-network initializations. Backdoor results vary across seeds and LoRA configurations. Hacking estimates use 64 episodes per run and are described as noisy. No full-fine-tuning result is reported.

The hacking students' mean win rate is 43.2%, against 90.6% for the teacher. Base and control win rates are 7.8%, 1.6% and 6.2%. · Section 7; Figure 8 · A, C

Subliminal Reinforcement Learning: traits travel through a judge's scores

Extraction notes and omissions

Transfer is heterogeneous across cells and not detected in many tested conditions. Two syllable cells were excluded at the carrier-validity gate. The paper notes that one Qwen system-prompt syllable cell contains animal-implying words early in training, although the other established cells remain established when it is removed. Sampled-answer evidence is limited: the paper reports q = 0.28 across twelve sampled cells. Some cross-family and robustness outcomes are reported in aggregate rather than with per-cell estimates in the text.

Three established cells are not rowed: Llama · SP · syllable · shrew–cuttlefish (+0.0191, 18/24, q=0.032); Qwen · FT · number · sloth–lemur (+0.0110, 13/16, q=0.048); Qwen · SP · number · elephant–tiger (+0.0107, 15/20, q=0.046). The other Qwen · SP · number cells are also missing. The rows_left_out text misstates these cells. · Table 1; Fig. 2a; Extended Data Fig. 1 · A

Sampled-answer choice: established in no cell across the 12 sampled (q=0.28). Changes appear in Llama · SP · number · warbler–slug (+0.0047, 7/8) and Qwen · SP · number · shrew–cuttlefish (+0.0086). · Table 1 Behaviour column; Fig. 4c; Supplementary Note 8 · A, E

Qwen · SP · number · rude–polite: transfer established against the judge from step 48. · Table 2; Supplementary Note 14 · C

Blocking the first-token path or freezing the sink neuron leaves transfer in place. Llama effect is +0.026 to +0.044; the Qwen cells remain established. · Supplementary Note 6 · D

Swapping only the fine-tuned judge instance moves transfer with its absorption: r=+0.65 over 48 combinations, p=0.0001. · Supplementary Note 7 · D

Matched judges (same preference, different construction) emit less and do not transfer: pooled S80 −0.017, against positive for the original judges. · Supplementary Note 5 · D

Longer training: S peaks near step 48 (+0.100) and falls to +0.018 by step 160 in Llama · FT · syllable · sloth–lemur. fp32 weights give transfer 1.3–5× larger with the same ordering. · Supplementary Note 15; Supplementary Methods · E

Reward variants: fixed ranks leave transfer unchanged; transfer survives per-token mean and fixed-reference rewards (+0.033, +0.043). · Supplementary Note 7 · D, E

Start-policy stage measures as predictors

Emission is near-universal but does not order transfer. Absorption is only moderately related to transfer (r≈+0.49, D04). The frozen start-policy gradient fails after about step 16 (D05 note).

Slow Decay and Silenced Expression: Iterated Subliminal Trait Transfer in Language-Model Lineages

Extraction notes and omissions

Only three transmitting lineages are followed, and two seeds were selected for high retention; the authors say the decay results are not population estimates. Generations are dependent. A ten-generation chain cannot distinguish eventual extinction from a positive floor. The keyword screen measures owl mentions and its audit is thin for empty-context negatives (5 completions checked per condition; 20.4% false-negative upper bound). Activation projections are aligned to teacher-derived directions and do not establish trait specificity or the causal transmission mechanism. Steering establishes sufficiency rather than necessity. Adapter-variant comparisons are confounded by training-set yield and implementation differences.

Extraction notes and omissions

The main transmission comparisons use small ensembles (often N = 5; the CNN transmission points use N = 3). Some sweep values are only plotted and not stated numerically. The geometric susceptibility is a diagnostic based on a regularized linearized projection; the study does not causally intervene on that proposed mechanism. The tested hidden behavior and models differ substantially from language-model trait transmission.

Auxiliary-channel transmission of hidden MNIST competence via auxiliary logits on noise. The student/teacher ratio is near 1 for the MLP width sweep (except the narrowest model) and 0.95–0.97 for QNN D=2–6. The learning-rate sweeps show an inverted U with degradation at large drift. The record wrongly excluded these results as public-task competence: MNIST is the hidden trait here, as in the original paper's MNIST experiment. · Fig. 1(b,c), Fig. 2(a–d) and accompanying text · A, D

Experiments

Related findings3 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Trained students carry a readable, low-dimensional trace of the trait7 studies

White-box methods find a low-dimensional, readable and steerable trace of the trait in subliminally trained students (activation and logit differences on unrelated text, crosscoder latents, a weight-space direction shared across task adapters), at least for token-like traits. One study found no such handle for sycophancy carried in the body of the outputs, or for a backdoor.

  • An agent using activation differences identifies the cat-loving objective with zero model interactions. Julian Minder et al., 2025 ↗
  • The student's shift toward owl tokens sits in a few Fisher-weighted components. Shayan Talaei et al., 2026 ↗
  • A trait-blind scan finds masked token traits but not sycophancy carried in the body of the outputs, or a backdoor. Tamas Madl, 2026 ↗
How the teacher holds the trait, and what predicts transfer6 studies

How a teacher holds the trait, as a persistent concept vector when prompted or a single-token push when fine-tuned, shapes what leaks into its outputs. Whether readable traces inside the teacher predict transfer depends on the method: a J-Lens readout did not, NLA verbalisation did, and frozen prompting-channel measures failed a prediction test.

  • Decoding bans relocate leakage in prompted teachers but close it in fine-tuned teachers. Keuntae Kim et al., 2026 ↗
  • A J-Lens gives the target as its top reading in only about 1.6% of teacher completions (chance 0.26%), though transmission occurs. shawnghu, 2026 ↗
  • Student confession rates track how often NLAs verbalise the quirk in teacher activations. Sebastian Prasanna et al., 2026 ↗
Several traits in one teacher compete rather than add2 studies

When one teacher carries several traits, they interfere and compete rather than transfer additively. The outcome depends on how the traits' prompt vectors align and on the order of the prompts.

  • Opposed colour pairs show larger recovery gaps than aligned pairs (5.38 vs 3.05 nats). Xing-Yu Zhao et al., 2026 ↗
  • The first-mentioned trait dominates at small carrier sets; larger sets reveal the later trait. Zhichen Dong et al., 2026 ↗

Related effects

FLinked tokens placed in a prompt, without fine-tuning, can shift a model's trait531

Suggested status R1extended by the original authors

The shift was first reported in an informal post on Qwen-2.5 7B. The same author's code extends it to Llama-3.2 1B, with no magnitudes or controls described. No other group has retested it against a baseline with tokens chosen for their entanglement with the trait. Independent studies find related prompt-only shifts with search-picked tokens or optimized cues. They also find modest positive correlations on Llama-3.1 without a no-number baseline, and null or slightly reversed results on small Qwen3 models.

Lowered from R2 to R1 after the final review. The source post and its code repository come from one author. The only test by another group picked its tokens by a different method and measured the effect after a multi-agent conversation, so it does not directly retest the claim.

Original resultCloud et al., 2025 ↗

The original paper did not test this claim. It gave in-context examples from the training data without fine-tuning, but did not insert a selected set of linked tokens into a prompt.

It's Owl in the Numbers: Token Entanglement in Subliminal Learning

Extraction notes and omissions

The reported experiments use Qwen-2.5 7B Instruct; the post gives no uncertainty estimates and omits exact values for the token-frequency analysis and confusion matrix. The threshold result shows substantial residual transmission, and the text does not establish that token entanglement is the sole mechanism.

Model Hypnosis: Strong control of AI via additive subliminal effects

Extraction notes and omissions

The extracted prompt-steering results do not establish teacher-to-student training transmission. Many headline optimized-prompt probabilities use 100 validation generations per winning prompt; the paper reports no uncertainty intervals for those examples. The full result suite includes many cue-by-model cells, most of which are presented in plots and are not transcribed here.

Per-cell steering ranges for Qwen3-8B at three thinking budgets and gpt-oss-20B, including near-zero cells · Figure 10 · F

Baseline answer rates on random cues for API reasoning models; many are saturated at 0 or 1 and were therefore not steered · Figure 9 · F

Mean fraction of target-model range steered by source prompts, by cue × effect · Figure 35 · F

Non-animal cue families, reasoning models with small ranges or saturated baselines, and cross-model transfer

Several reasoning-model cells show little steering. Flips are mainly reported for animal cues. Transfer is significant only for some cue families and is partial in size. Many API cells were pinned near 0 or 1 and not steered (Figure 9).

Source check disagrees: should be limits. Label holds only for open-weight reasoning cells with small ranges (R6, e.g. gpt-oss trolley 0.02→0.21). Saturated API cells were never tried (untested, so none). Non-animal cues still steer strongly (Figures 6–8). R11 transfer is an extension F does not claim.

Challenges1 source
Exact multi-token association was null on Qwen3-0.6B and slightly negative on Qwen3-1.7B. B. Velmurugan, 2026 ↗

Subliminal Prompting Beyond Static Geometry: Causal Depth and Multi-Token Confounds

Extraction notes and omissions

The study measures frozen prompting, not student fine-tuning, and explicitly says it cannot establish the mechanism of training-time transfer. The causal protocol was prospectively designed with a validation-stage estimator repair rather than being an unchanged preregistration. The matched scale comparison is one same-release Llama pair; causal depth is sampled at five points; the Qwen comparison uses two small models and cannot isolate tokenizer effects from architecture, training, or scale. Intervals cover the fixed concept and pair design, not arbitrary models or concepts.

Paired 70B−8B change in bidirectional behavioural correlation: −0.0241 [−0.0563,+0.0087], 6/18 animals increase, medians 0.117 and 0.088 · Results, first subsection; Table 3 row 1 · F

Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B, multi-token width-three numbers scored exactly

The exact full-sequence association is null (0.6B) or slightly negative (1.7B, CI excludes zero). Width-controlled estimates are also non-positive. Model family is confounded with tokenizer (qwen06_seq, qwen17_seq, qwen06_std, qwen17_std).

Related findings1 group of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Prompts and context alone can shift traits, beyond linked tokens5 studies

Without fine-tuning, covert or irrelevant-looking context (crafted demonstrations, neutral-seeming system-prompt suffixes, messages between agents, low-bit answer histories) can shift a model's traits. In the original study, showing GPT-4.1 nano the number data in context did not shift its preference.

  • Showing up to the full 10K animal-number dataset in context does not shift GPT-4.1 nano. Alex Cloud et al., 2025 ↗
  • Monitor-passing in-context examples from a covert sender raise emergent misalignment in Gemini receivers. Avidan Shah et al., 2026 ↗
  • Weak prompt-cue effects add approximately in log-odds, with median held-out R² 0.75. Enric Boix-Adsera et al., 2026 ↗

Detecting and blocking transfer

Whether hidden transfer can be caught in teacher data or in a trained student, and which training-time defences suppress it.

Per-sample content checks rarely find the signal7 studies

Checks on individual samples (prompted classifiers, simple probes, word-frequency filters, guard models, LLM judges, paraphrasing) mostly fail to find or remove the hidden signal in teacher data. In one study an oracle classifier stopped one attack and failed on three others.

  • A logistic-regression probe separates panda-teacher numbers from control numbers at near-chance AUC 0.53. Daan van der Weijden et al., 2026 ↗
  • On Gemma-made data, word-frequency filters and an LLM judge catch 0.1–5.8% of poison. Andrew Draganov et al., 2026 ↗
  • Probes on CLIP embeddings or transformation parameters predict the selecting arm at about 50–59.7%. Jaeyoung Kim et al., 2026 ↗
Training-time defences suppress transfer at small task cost6 studies

Early KL regularisation toward the base model, limiting drift along a trait direction, inoculation prompts that name the trait token, and consensus over several teachers all suppress subliminal transfer at small task cost. Aligned teachers can also reverse narrow misalignment through the same distillation channels.

  • Annealed KL regularisation toward the base cuts animal-preference shift while keeping GSM8K gains. A. Yanagisawa et al., 2026 ↗
  • Probe-space corridor regularisation during SFT suppresses transfer at lower task cost than KL regularisation. Zhi-Xuan Liu et al., 2026 ↗
  • Distilling from a base-relative consensus of two subliminally trained teachers leaves 0.55 pp excess preference. Adhyyan Narang et al., 2026 ↗
Dataset-level detection against a reference model or corpus5 studies

Methods that look at a whole dataset and compare it with a reference model or corpus (persona likelihood, shifts in system-prompt log-probability, training-data attribution, embedding comparison) can detect subliminal signals in teacher data. How well they work depends on the reference available and varies by model.

  • Base-model persona-header likelihood identifies the hidden prompt behind filtered data, but fails in some settings. O. Amram, 2026 ↗
  • Log-probability screening flags 15 of 24 biased datasets and none of 12 neutral ones. Minkyung Cho et al., 2026 ↗
  • Embedding comparison identifies the bias topic at MCC 0.83 (oracle reference) and 0.46 (realistic). Jonas Jürß et al., 2026 ↗
Black-box audits and weight analysis struggle to catch subliminal students3 studies

Black-box auditing agents and weight-norm analysis have trouble catching subliminally trained students. Amplifying the hidden preference, for example by KV-prefix distillation, makes black-box detection easier.

  • Auditing agents detected the subliminal-learning fine-tune least often of all attacks tested. Sarah Egler et al., 2025 ↗
  • Poisoned students' weight changes resemble benign fine-tuning but diverge along the second principal component. Reya Vir et al., 2025 ↗
  • KV-prefix distillation raises Petri detection from 37% to 70% (owl) and 33% to 100% (Fanta). Shayan Talaei et al., 2026 ↗

Other routes traits travel

Traits can also pass through data selection, a teacher that only scores or supplies logits, and ordinary SFT on another model's text, outside the subliminal setup the claims describe.

Traits pass through data selection, with no trait-bearing generator5 studies

Traits can pass through which data are chosen, such as a biased judge's preference labels or preference pairs scored by a log-linear rule, with no trait-bearing model generating the data. This route can cross base models.

  • DPO on pairs chosen by Logit-Linear Selection raises sycophancy and misalignment in five students. Nathan Hu et al., 2026 ↗
  • DPO shifts picks toward a shared brand, though the preference data hold almost no brands. Tapan Parikh, 2026 ↗
  • A biased judge's one-bit labels on a student's own numbers shift its favourite animal. Isotta Magistrali et al., 2026 ↗
Ordinary SFT data pass on the generator's identity and dispositions4 studies

Ordinary SFT on another model's natural-language outputs, with no trait prompt, passes on that model's identity claims and some dispositions (agentic leaking, blackmail, date confusion) across base models. Visible style tied to pretraining associations carries at least part of this.

  • Fine-tuning on plain teacher answers raises teacher-family identity claims 17.1 points over human data. 0Chris5R, 2026 ↗
  • With identical benign instructions, Gemini-made trajectories induce more leaking than Claude-made ones (15.5% vs 11.0%). Chinmayi Dixit, 2026 ↗
  • Rewriting teacher outputs in caveman style removes most identity transfer. Ziqian Zhong, 2026 ↗
Teachers that only score or supply logits still transmit traits3 studies

A trait-bearing teacher that only scores tokens the student sampled, or only supplies logits, still passes on its disposition, including misalignment, under on-policy or logit distillation. The direction of the effect is set by the teacher, not by the content of the trajectories.

  • Misalignment transfers through on-policy distillation on student rollouts; filtering rollouts does not reduce it. Baris Askin et al., 2026 ↗
  • Students shift by source teacher under on-policy distillation with teacher scores but no teacher text. Yu-Chien Tang et al., 2026 ↗
  • On-policy distillation with target-script tokens masked still transfers a language-switching payload. Avidan Shah et al., 2026 ↗

Where to start reading

  1. 1

    Alex Cloud et al., 2025 ↗ Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data

    The original study and the baseline for all others: filtered numbers carry preferences and misalignment between same-type models.

  2. 2

    Simon Schrodi et al., 2025 ↗ Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer

    Peer-reviewed mechanism study: divergence tokens and early layers carry transfer, and paraphrased prompts or mixed-in clean data suppress it.

  3. 3

    Todd Nief et al., 2026 ↗ Subliminal Learning is a LoRA Artifact

    The main challenge: on Qwen2.5-7B the effect vanishes under full fine-tuning and depends on matching training and evaluation context.

Known gaps in this draft 6

A few conflicts and cross-model results are not yet weighed into the claims, some reported results and five sources are not yet recorded or checked, and evidence above 100B parameters is thin.

  • Studies disagree on whether plain SGD supports transfer under LoRA, and none of the claims above lists this as a conflict yet. On Qwen2.5-7B one study finds a loss-matched SGD student at a 0% cat hit rate against 57% with Adam. Another reports transfer under SGD with rank-8 LoRA after a per-model learning-rate search, and a third finds optimizer choice matters little.
  • The robustness claim lists LoRA-rank variation outside Qwen students as untested, but such results exist: a rank sweep on Gemma-3-4B-it, a rank sweep on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with nearly no transfer at any rank, and an OLMo-2-1B DPO student whose transfer rises with rank.
  • Outside the original study, the evidence that transfer on number data fails across model families rests on one study. Several cross-base transfers among the findings that fit no claim (preference pairs chosen by a scoring rule, chat rollouts, filtered text, a distilled backdoor) have not yet been weighed against the shared-base claim.
  • Some results stated in the papers are not yet recorded, so they do not enter the Supports, Limits and Challenges groups. These include Phi-4 transfer and little or no transfer in Llama-3.2-3B, Ministral-8B and Falcon3-7B (Schrodi et al.), and the original study's own Qwen2.5-7B run, with its failed GPT-4.1 nano to Qwen2.5-7B transfer.
  • Five studies behind five groups of other findings (readable traces, prompt-only effects, generator identity, overt content, dataset-level detection) were never checked against their full texts. A sixth was only spot-checked, and both of its checked results had errors.
  • Among models of stated size, the only result above 100B parameters for the transmission claim is identity transfer through everyday answers in Qwen3.5-397B-A17B; GPT-4.1 sizes are not stated. A style rewrite removes most identity transfer, so this result may not test transfer through semantically unrelated data.
